label: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017
output:
**One Assignment**

Jess texted me last night: “It’s one assignment. Don’t torch your job over it.” Then half the group chat agreed with her, and I went to bed annoyed at nobody in particular. I’m not writing this to win the chat. I’d rather explain myself once, properly, than send fifteen texts that all start with “ok but.”

So here’s the short version. I teach juniors at Cobb Street High—US History II, two sections. For four years I’ve assigned a busing oral history project. Kids interview someone in their family or neighborhood about Boston between 1974 and 1976, record about ten minutes, and write a two-page reflection. Four years, never a complaint. Then a parent emailed Dr. Halvorsen and cc’d a school committee member. She said the project “reopens wounds” and “pressures kids to judge their grandparents.” Halvorsen wants me to quietly drop it. I’m not going to. I meet with him and the parent Thursday, November 19, at 3:15.

I want to be clear about what “not dropping it” means. It does not mean I’m walking in with a PowerPoint called “Why I’m Right.” It means I’m keeping the assignment and adding a real alternate option. No kid has to interview family. They can interview a librarian or an archivist, or use recorded interviews from past years with permission. That’s not a fig leaf. It’s a better version of the project. If a kid doesn’t want to sit across from Grandma and ask about busing, they shouldn’t have to. I actually think the parent has a point about the pressure. A kid shouldn’t feel like they have to cross-examine their own family for a grade. What I’m not willing to do is pretend the whole subject is too hot to touch.

Because this is literally the history of the city they live in. The textbook gives it one paragraph. One. And most of these kids have families who were here in 1974, or got here because of what happened after. The project isn’t about making anybody feel bad. It’s about the fact that history is not a paragraph. It’s the stuff your grandmother won’t talk about at dinner.

In 2023 a kid—I’ll call him D.—interviewed his grandmother, who drove a school bus in Southie in ’74. She had never told anyone in the family. Not her kids, not her husband. D. played forty seconds of the recording for the class and nobody said a word for about a minute. Not a cough. I’ve never had a silence like that in a classroom before or since.

Last year a girl found out her uncle threw rocks at a bus. She was upset. We talked after class twice—once that day, once a week later. Her reflection was the best thing I read all year. I’m not going to quote it because it’s hers, but she wrote about how you can love somebody and still know they did something wrong. She got there herself. I didn’t get her there.

That’s the thing I keep coming back to. The kids who are uncomfortable are the ones who need it most, but I don’t get to force anyone. That’s the line. The parent is right that there’s pressure. I’m fixing that with the alternate. What I’m not doing is deciding the subject itself is the problem.

I don’t think the parent is a villain. I don’t know her. Her email was polite, as far as these things go. She’s worried about her kid. I’m worried about all of them. Those can both be true.

Jess, I know why you sent that text. You’re not wrong that I could get burned. I’m tenured—since 2021—so it’s not a firing thing, at least not in the way people mean. But Halvorsen controls my schedule and who gets AP. I like my schedule. I like teaching AP. I’m not pretending that’s nothing. I’m a little scared, honestly. I’m not brave about this. I’m just not willing to make this the thing I fold on.

You left teaching in 2019 and went into HR at a biotech in Cambridge, so I know you’re looking at this from a different angle. You see how institutions protect themselves. You’re probably right about how this could go. But you also know me. We met student teaching in 2012 at the same school. You’ve watched me turn a simple thing into a principle before. This isn’t that. Or it is, but it’s also just the assignment.

I’m not picking a fight with the parent. I’m not trying to make Halvorsen look bad. I’m going to walk into that meeting with the alternate option written down, and I’m going to listen. If she has a better idea for how to keep the history without the pressure, I’ll take it. I’m not wedded to the exact assignment. I’m wedded to the kids learning that this city’s history is not a paragraph.

Maybe I’m wrong about how this goes. Maybe Halvorsen says no and I have to decide what happens next. I don’t know yet. But I know I’m not going to quietly drop it before the meeting and then pretend I did it for pedagogical reasons. That’s the version of this I couldn’t live with.

Jess, I don’t need you to agree. I’d like you to understand why. The rest of you can keep texting; I’ll answer after Thursday.

I’ll text you Thursday after the meeting, Jess. Probably from the parking lot. Probably before I start the car.
